newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian stocks firm in rising turnover.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian stocks firm in rising turnover.

text.p: Hungarian stocks continued to rise on Wednesday on reviving buying interest following central bank interest rate hikes in Hungary and the U.S. earlier this week, traders said.
The BUX index finished at 5,281.76 points, up 148.11 points, while spot share turnover rose to 2.559 billion forints, from Tuesday's 2.065 billion forints and Monday's 1.16 billion forints.

"The interest of foreigners has increased, and turnover (on the Budapest Stock Exchange) rose substantially in the past three days," said ABN-Amro Hoare Govett's Gregory Osztrovszky. "The reaction to the U.S. interest rate hike was favourable."

Traders said the Fed's move on Tuesday to raise its funds rate by 0.25 of a percentage point was widely expected and its impact had been built into Hungarian share prices in the past three weeks, but the eventual rate hike relieved the bourse from psychological pressure.

London-based Merril Lynch analyst Tom Chadwick said Hungary was the most closely linked central European aconomy to the U.S. market but he did not see a strong correlation between the Fed rate hike and the Budapest bourse.
He added that Hungarian shares received an impetus from the National Bank of Hungary's 0.25 percent surprise hike in the six-month deposit rate to 21 percent on Monday.
"From the western point of view this is an extremely welcome development," he said.

"First of all, it encourages the high domestic savings level and takes inflationary pressure out of the market," he added. "But it also gives the international investors a great deal of confidence that tis government is committed to keeping inflation under control."
Traders said the increasing interest of foreigners was felt, but most stocks were still illiquid as sellers waited for higher price levels.
They added that price rises following the past three week's downward correction wave were not surprising, but they were not sure that a new rising trend had begun on Tuesday.
However, traders and analysts said the BSE's longer term outlook was positive.
"The market was due a correction," said Chadwick. "But having drawn breath, it is beginning to show signs of the momentum continuing."
He added that Hungary expected a recovery of domestic demand and this improved the outlook of the BSE.
"As the pace of the consumer recovery begins to grow, you can expect to see some recovery in domestic oriented stocks, which until now have been second tier to the export-oriented stocks."
